Nothing here is generated at runtime. The study covers type 2 diabetes only. Local-language triggers are included because many users in South Cotabato speak Hiligaynon or Cebuano; a native speaker should review them before the defence.

topics.answer: Vomiting, stomach pain, fast or deep breathing, fruity-smelling breath, or unusual drowsiness or confusion, especially with great thirst and frequent urination, can mean a hyperglycaemic emergency — diabetic ketoacidosis or a hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state. Both are medical emergencies and the second is more common in type 2. Go to an emergency department or call 911 now. Do not wait and do not finish the assessment first.

Diabetes means blood glucose stays too high. In type 2, which is what this system covers and by far the most common form, the body still makes insulin but responds to it poorly, and over the years the pancreas cannot keep up with the extra demand. Other forms exist and are managed differently; which one a person has is a clinician's judgement.

Type 2 diabetes is a progressive loss of the body's ability to use insulin well, usually alongside a gradual decline in how much the pancreas can produce. It often develops over years without symptoms, which is why screening matters: by the time thirst or blurred vision appear, glucose has usually been high for some time. It can often be delayed or prevented, and it can be managed.

The common early signs are heavy thirst, passing urine much more often, losing weight without trying, tiredness, blurred vision and constant hunger. None is specific on its own, which is why a glucose test matters.

HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over roughly three months. The published diagnostic cut-off is 6.5 percent or above, and 5.7 to 6.4 percent is the intermediate range. It shows that glucose is abnormal, not which type of diabetes it is.

A fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or above, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or above with classic symptoms, meets the diagnostic threshold. Fasting 100 to 125 mg/dL is the intermediate range. Unless glucose is unmistakably high, one result has to be confirmed by a second test before it counts as a diagnosis.

Prediabetes is glucose that is higher than normal but not yet at the diagnostic cut-off: a fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL, a 2-hour value of 140 to 199, or an HbA1c of 5.7 to 6.4 per cent. It is the stage type 2 diabetes passes through, it usually has no symptoms, and it is the point at which changes to diet and activity do the most good. It is a reason to act, not a diagnosis.

A parent or sibling with type 2 diabetes is one of the risk factors the ADA lists as a reason to be tested earlier than age 35. It raises risk substantially, and it is one of the most common reasons someone in this study would qualify for screening. It is not a sentence: most people with an affected relative do not go on to develop it, and the things that lower risk are the same things that help anyway. No figure specific to the Philippines is available here, so none is quoted.

Often, yes — and many people assume the opposite, which is worth correcting. For adults at high risk, the ADA recommends a diabetes prevention programme aiming at a weight reduction of at least 5 to 7 per cent, together with regular physical activity. In the Diabetes Prevention Program trial, that approach cut new cases by about 58 per cent over roughly three years, more than the medicine arm did. Eating sugar is not the single cause, and blame is not useful, but diet, activity and weight are genuinely things that change the odds.

Type 2 diabetes is managed with changes to diet and activity, often with medicine — metformin is usually the first — and sometimes with insulin later on. Which of those applies to anyone is a doctor's decision and I cannot advise on it. What I can say is that it is manageable, that early action makes a real difference, and that people with type 2 diabetes live full lives.

No model has been trained for this project yet, so there is no accuracy figure to report. The assessment compares your entries against published diagnostic thresholds instead. When a model exists, its measured metrics will appear on the Research and evaluation page, and never before.

No model has been trained. The study has not secured a dataset drawn from a population comparable to this one, and a model fitted to a foreign cohort would carry that cohort's base rates into South Cotabato without saying so. The ADA's screening and diagnostic criteria are already a published, validated rule, so the system applies those instead and shows you which cut-off your entry met. That is why you will never see a percentage here.

Forecasting future onset is not implemented. It needs longitudinal data, people followed over time with the date of diagnosis recorded, and the study does not have that. Case-versus-control data can only classify current status. The Risk forecasting page lists everything that would be required.

The result is a next-step recommendation, not a risk score or a diagnosis. It says whether anything you entered crosses a published threshold. There are five outcomes: emergency, see a doctor promptly, worth getting tested, not enough information, and nothing crosses a threshold. I cannot interpret your personal results; a clinician has to do that.

A result of nothing crosses a threshold is not an all-clear. Type 2 diabetes develops gradually, often over years, and usually without symptoms until glucose is already high, so a normal result describes today and not next year. The ADA's answer to that is repeat testing at least every three years, sooner if your risk factors change. Come back if thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, fatigue or slow-healing cuts appear or worsen.

Open the Testing centre map page. Records appear only after the research team verifies them, so the list may still be short. Every municipality in the Philippines operates a Rural Health Unit under the Local Government Code, so your municipal health office is the reliable starting point for a blood glucose test.

Each facility record carries its own source and verification date. Verified means someone confirmed it from an official directory, the facility website or a phone call, and logged the date. Unconfirmed means nobody has checked yet. Outdated means a recheck found something had changed. A service is never shown as confirmed without a source and a date behind it.

Ten municipalities in South Cotabato: Surallah, Sto. Nino, Lake Sebu, Norala, T'boli, Banga, Tampakan, Tantangan, Tupi and Polomolok. Facilities outside these are outside the study's defined mapping coverage.

The assessment collects no name, birth date, address or contact detail. Your answers go to the DiabetEASE server to compute the result and are then discarded, unless an operator explicitly enables storage and you consent. Even then the stored record holds a banded age and counts, never an exact age or an identifier, with a deletion date. The design follows the Data Privacy Act of 2012.

Open Risk assessment from the menu. Five steps: age and municipality, family history, symptoms, any laboratory results you already have, then a review before the outcome. Anything you do not know can be left blank, and blanks are treated as unknown, never as normal.

That is normal, and you can still complete the assessment. Without a laboratory value the result will say there is not enough information, which is the honest answer rather than a guess. A fasting or random blood glucose test is inexpensive and widely available, and it settles the question in a way this form cannot.

The study aims to design, develop and evaluate DiabetEASE: a multi-parameter Type 2 diabetes screening, testing centre mapping and decision-support system. It evaluates functional quality under ISO/IEC 25010, geographic information accuracy, and user acceptability.

It uses a developmental research design, in seven phases: requirements analysis, data acquisition and preprocessing, model development, system development, initial evaluation, usability evaluation and revision, then final evaluation and documentation.

It is a senior high school research project at Libertad National High School in Surallah, South Cotabato. No university, government agency or medical body endorses it, and it is not clinically validated.

The main ones: no trained model, so no probability is produced; no forecasting, because longitudinal data is not available; facility records depend on fieldwork and may go out of date; and the system cannot conduct laboratory tests, access medical equipment or perform clinical examinations. None of its output is a diagnosis.

I'm Candie, the DiabetEASE health assistant. I answer from a fixed list of reviewed explanations written by the research team, so I will not invent a medical claim. I can explain Type 2 diabetes, walk you through a result you have already recorded, and help you find your way around the site. I cannot diagnose anyone.

This system does not hold prices, and fees vary by facility. One thing worth knowing: PhilHealth's primary care package, now called YAKAP and formerly Konsulta, lists fasting blood sugar, the glucose tolerance test and HbA1c among its covered laboratory tests when your registered provider's doctor orders them. Ask your municipal health office how to register.

Blood glucose that stays high over years can damage the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart and blood vessels. Keeping glucose close to target greatly reduces that risk, which is why diagnosis and ongoing care matter. Short term, very high glucose with ketones can cause diabetic ketoacidosis, which is a medical emergency. A clinician manages all of this; this system does not.

PhilHealth's primary care package, YAKAP (called Konsulta before 2025), covers a check-up plus a set of laboratory tests that includes fasting blood sugar, the glucose tolerance test and HbA1c, ordered by the provider's doctor as needed. You register with one accredited provider. If that clinic has no laboratory, the test may be done at a partner laboratory, so an accredited facility on the map does not always run the test on site.

The ADA recommends testing every adult from age 35, and repeating it at least every three years while results stay normal. Below 35, testing is recommended for anyone with overweight or obesity who has at least one risk factor. The BMI cut-off for that is 23 rather than 25 for people of Asian ancestry — which includes this study's population — and Asian ancestry is itself one of the listed risk factors. In practice that means most adults here with a BMI of 23 or above should be tested, whatever their age.

The risk factors the ADA lists for earlier testing are: a first-degree relative with diabetes; high-risk ancestry, Asian ancestry included; a history of cardiovascular disease; high blood pressure at or above 130/80, or treatment for it; HDL cholesterol below 35 mg/dL or triglycerides above 250; physical inactivity; polycystic ovary syndrome; diabetes in a previous pregnancy; a previous result in the prediabetes range; and other conditions linked to insulin resistance. One is enough, if BMI is at or above the cut-off.
